sentences.text: Dorygnathus possessed a wingspan of approximately 1.5 metres.
This creature featured a long skull where the eye sockets were the largest openings, with the largest known specimen measuring sixteen centimetres in length and a lower jaw extending 147 millimetres.
Dorygnathus exhibited heterodonty, having different types of teeth, a condition rare in modern reptiles but common in primitive pterosaurs.
It remains unknown whether the tail of Dorygnathus possessed a diamond-shaped structure at its end, as seen in Rhamphorhynchus.
Ferdinand Broili reported the presence of fur on specimen BSP 1938 I 49, suggesting Dorygnathus had hair and a high metabolism.
The first remains of Dorygnathus were discovered near Banz, Bavaria, and described in 1830 by Carl Theodori.
The genus Dorygnathus was formally named by Johann Andreas Wagner in 1860.
The holotype of Dorygnathus is a lower jaw specimen designated PSB 757.
Rupert Wild described and named the second species Dorygnathus mistelgauensis in 1971.
Evidence from gut contents suggests that Dorygnathus was a piscivore, or fish-eater, and direct evidence includes gut contents containing the teleost fish Leptolepis.
Some specimens show tooth wear consistent with eating hard food items like crustaceans and mollusks.
The extreme length of Dorygnathus's front teeth allowed them to project beyond the head margins when the beak was closed, and the long front teeth of both jaws interlocked when the mouth closed.
The smallest known Dorygnathus specimen has a wingspan of sixty centimetres, and no juveniles are known.
Researcher Padian concluded that Dorygnathus grew rapidly as a juvenile and continued growing slowly after maturity, potentially reaching a wingspan of 1.7 metres.
On land, Dorygnathus was probably a poor climber as its claws show no special adaptations for that type of locomotion.
According to Padian, Dorygnathus was very capable of bipedal locomotion due to being a relatively small pterosaur with a long tail.
Baron Franz Nopcsa assigned Dorygnathus to the subfamily Rhamphorhynchinae in 1928, a classification confirmed by Peter Wellnhofer in 1978, and he also assigned Dimorphodon to this group.

Modern cladistic analyses have not reached a consensus on the exact relationships of Dorygnathus, with David Unwin placing it in Rhamphorhynchinae while Alexander Kellner placed it in a more basal position.
Most pterosaur researchers agree that all pterosaurs were quadrupeds, contrasting with Padian's view on Dorygnathus.
